1kn21c6:256: The essence of context engineering is solving the attention dilution problem. Transformer attention complexity is O(n²); the longer the context, the more easily key signals get diluted by noise, and Context Rot is the most common failure mode. The solution is layered management by information usage frequency and stability: the resident layer (identity definition, project conventions, absolute prohibitions) stays short, hard, and executable; the on-demand loading layer (Skills and domain knowledge) keeps descriptors resident and injects full content only when triggered; the runtime injection layer (current time, channel ID, user preferences) is assembled per turn as needed; the memory layer (cross-session experience) does not enter the system prompt directly and is only read when needed; the system layer (Hooks or code rules) handles deterministic logic and never enters context.

1tzyeqq:277: The core issue in multi-Agent collaboration is not parallelism but isolation and collaboration patterns. There are two working modes: commander mode (a human interacts closely with a single Agent, adjusting decisions every turn, and artifacts disappear when the session ends) and coordinator mode (a human appears at the start and end, while multiple Agents work in parallel in between, producing persistent artifacts such as PRs). Collaboration requires protocols to be written clearly first (structured messages, stateful, append-only, crash-recoverable), task graphs and dependencies defined upfront, and isolation boundaries established first (sub-Agents have independent messages[] and only return summaries; exploration details stay in the sub-Agent's own context). In multi-Agent settings, hallucinations amplify each other, so cross-validation is needed to break the error propagation chain.

7slti6:216: Agent evaluation structure is far more complex than traditional evaluation: tools, runtime environments, and tasks must be prepared first; during execution the Agent calls tools multiple times to modify environment state; final scoring does not look at what it said but runs tests to verify what actually happened in the environment. Common sources of errors in evaluation systems include insufficient runtime environment resources causing processes to be killed, the scorer itself having bugs that mark correct answers as failures, test cases disconnected from production scenarios, or only looking at aggregate scores while missing systematic degradation in a category of tasks—these all look identical to model degradation in terms of performance. The correct order is: check the environment first, then touch the Agent.
9wvhcg:236: One of the article's core points: model capability certainly matters, but what determines whether a system runs stably is often the surrounding engineering conditions. This judgment holds most strongly for highly verifiable tasks like code writing—OpenAI used 3 engineers and 5 months to write a million lines of code across nearly 1,500 PRs, 10 times faster than traditional development. Behind this is not how strong the model is, but that the Harness engineering was done right: what the Agent cannot see does not exist (knowledge must live in the codebase itself), constraints are codified rather than documented (architecture layering is mechanically enforced through custom Linters), and tasks are completed end-to-end autonomously (from verification to merge, the full chain requires no human intervention).

vqe9bi:303: Tool design has gone through three stages: first-generation API wrappers (granularity too fine; the Agent must coordinate multiple tools to complete a goal) → second-generation ACI (Agent-Computer Interface; tools correspond to Agent goals rather than underlying API operations) → third-generation Advanced Tool Use (Tool Search for dynamic discovery, Programmatic Tool Calling for code orchestration, Tool Use Examples for example-driven usage). The core of ACI principles: tool descriptions state when to use and when not to use, errors are structured with corrective suggestions, and definitions are bound to implementations. When debugging an Agent, check tool definitions first, because most tool selection errors come from inaccurate descriptions, not model capability.
